Thus have I heard:
At one time the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in his robes and taken up his alms bowl at the hour of eating, entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having completed his alms-round through the city in due order, he returned to his original location; after finishing his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and as was his custom, spread out his seat and sat cross-legged. He remained with body upright, dwelling in right mindfulness, unmoving.
"At that time, the bhikṣus came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, being amidst the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and stood before the Buddha with palms joined in reverence, addressing the Buddha: [...]"
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
The Commentary says:
"Skillfully protecting and mindful" refers to bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature.
"Skillfully entrusting" refers to bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature.
How does one skillfully protect and mindfully care for bodhisattvas?
How are bodhisattvas well-entrusted?
The verse says:
One should know that skillful protection of the meaning consists in augmenting their bodies and acting in concert with them.
Not losing what has been attained and attaining what has not yet been attained—this is called "the excellent entrustment.
What is meant by "augmenting their bodies and acting in concert"?
It refers to bestowing the power of wisdom within the bodies of bodhisattvas, so that they may accomplish the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva embraces sentient beings and bestows upon them the power of transformation; this should be known as "skillful protection and mindfulness.
What is meant by "not regressing from what has been attained or not yet attained"?
This refers to entrusting those who have already attained or have not yet attained spiritual qualities to wise persons out of fear that they might lose them.
Furthermore, for those who have attained non-retrogression, it is because they do not abandon the Mahāyāna;
for those who have not yet attained non-retrogression, it is because one desires to cause them to excel and progress within the Mahāyāna. This should be understood as "skillful entrustment."

“‘World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva, having resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the Mahāyāna, abide? How should they dwell?’”
"How should one practice?
How should one subdue the mind?
At that time, the Buddha told Subhūti:
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
It is as you have said: the Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.”
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
As for a Bodhisattva in the Mahāyāna who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should abide in this way, practice in this way, and subdue their mind in this way.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so; I wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All bodhisattvas give rise to this thought:

'Of all sentient beings included within the realm of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all sentient beings included within the realm of sentient beings—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.'"
"In this way, although he brings immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva perceives the mark of a sentient being, they are not a bodhisattva.
Why is it that they are not? Subhūti!
"If a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, they are not called a bodhisattva.

This meaning is demonstrated through a dialogue.

Vast, foremost, and eternal, his mind is not inverted.
"Abiding in the profound mind of benefit, the merit of this vehicle is fulfilled.
What meaning does this verse express?
If a bodhisattva possesses four kinds of profound and beneficial bodhicitta, these constitute the bodhisattva’s dwelling place within the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Because the merit of this profound mind is fulfilled, four kinds of profound benefit arise within the mind, enabling one to abide within the Mahāyāna.

What is the benefit of a broad mind?

As it is said in the Sūtra: "All Bodhisattvas give rise to such a thought: 'All sentient beings whatsoever who are included within the category of sentient beings, even unto all those included within the realm of sentient beings...'"
What is the benefit of the foremost mind?
It is as the sutra says: "I shall cause all to abide in nirvana without remainder and thereby bring them to extinction.
What is the benefit of the constant mind?
As it is said in the Sūtra: "In this way, although immeasurable and boundless sentient beings are brought to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Subhūti!"
"If a bodhisattva perceives the mark of a sentient being, they are not a bodhisattva.
What is the meaning of this?
A bodhisattva regards all sentient beings as if they were their own body.
For this reason, when the Bodhisattva himself attains parinirvāṇa, there is no other sentient being who attains parinirvāṇa.
If a Bodhisattva conceives the notion of "sentient beings" toward others while not giving rise to the notion of "self," then he should not be called by the name "Bodhisattva."
Thus, regarding sentient beings as one's own body and never abandoning them is called benefiting with a constant mind.
What is benefiting with a non-perverted mind?
As it is said in the Sūtra: "For what reason?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, he is not called a bodhisattva. Thus it is taught.
This is shown because it demonstrates the distancing from the characteristics of sentient beings who rely upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

From this point onward, the practice of how a bodhisattva dwells within the Mahāyāna is explained.
This matter should be understood.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on things; he practices giving without dwelling anywhere:
he does not dwell on form when practicing giving, nor does he dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, not dwelling on perceptions of signs. Why is that?
If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, the mass of their merit cannot be measured or conceived.
Subhūti, what do you think?
“Can the space of the eastern direction be measured?
Subhūti replied, “No, [it cannot].”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “It is so.”
"Subhūti! Can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! The mass of merit of a bodhisattva who practices giving without abiding in signs is likewise immeasurable and inconceivable."
The Buddha further addressed Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner alone.
The Commentary says:
The verse says:
The meaning of *dāna* (giving) encompasses six types: material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma;
among these, one, two, and three are called the stages of cultivation and abiding.
For what reason is it that only the *dānapāramitā* is designated as "the teaching of the six *pāramitās*"?
Because all *pāramitās* are manifested through the characteristics and meaning of the *dānapāramitā*.

Regarding the meaning of the characteristics of all *pāramitās* as generosity (*dāna*), it should be understood that these consist of the *pāramitās* of material generosity, fearlessness, and the Dharma.
What is the meaning of this?
The "giving of material goods" (*āmiṣadāna*) is so named because it is the essence of the single *dānapāramitā*.
Regarding the "giving of fearlessness" (*abhayadāna*), there are two types:
namely, the *śīlapāramitā* and the *kṣāntipāramitā*, because through them one does not give rise to fear regarding evil deeds already committed or yet to be committed.
The dharma-dāna pāramitā has three aspects:
namely, being untiring in the vīrya-pāramitā and the others, skillfully knowing the mind, and preaching the Dharma in accordance with reality.
This is precisely the dwelling of the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
As previously stated, the three kinds of *dāna* encompass the six *pāramitās*; this is called the dwelling of the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
How does a bodhisattva practice giving without dwelling on things?
To this effect, the verse says:
Regarding one's own self, the desire for gratitude, And the karmic fruit of retribution—one is unattached to these.
Protecting oneself and not practicing giving, one guards against seeking other matters.
"Not abiding in things" means not being attached to one's own person.
"Having nothing on which to abide" means not being attached to the repayment of kindness.
Requiting gratitude refers to various modes such as making offerings and showing respect, as stated in the Sūtra: "because there is no dwelling.
Not dwelling in form and so forth means not being attached to karmic retribution.
For what reason does one thus not abide [in attachment] while practicing generosity?
The verse says: "To protect oneself, one does not give; to prevent seeking other matters. If one is attached to one's own person, one does not practice generosity;
therefore, in order to protect against this, one is not attached to the body.
If one clings to the repayment of gratitude, the karmic fruit will cause one to abandon the Buddha’s bodhi; thus, one practices giving for the sake of a different purpose.
To prevent such conduct, one does not cling to the object [of the gift].
From here on below, it will be explained how a bodhisattva subdues his mind;
this matter should be understood.
How is it that subduing the mind is called "subduing"?
The verse says:
In the task of subduing those [afflictions], one should distance oneself from the mind that grasps at signs,
sever various doubts, and likewise prevent the arising of conceptualizing thoughts.
What is the meaning of this passage?
It refers to not perceiving the gift, the recipient, or the donor.
As the verse says:
In the matter of subduing those [afflictions], one remains far removed from the mind that grasps at signs.
As the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this way, not dwelling on the perception of signs."
Next, the benefits of giving are explained.
Why is this? Because there is doubt regarding this matter:
If one were free from the conceptualization of the marks of giving and so forth, how could the merit of giving be accomplished?
Because for such a person, giving in this manner results in even greater merit.
Next, the benefits of giving are explained.
As the sutra says: "For what reason?
If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, the mass of his merit cannot be measured or conceived. Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Can the space in the eastern direction be measured? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! and so forth.
Why is it that after explaining the practice of cultivation, the benefits of giving are next revealed?
Because one has attained mastery over the mind, the benefits of giving are therefore explained next.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that one practices giving while not dwelling on signs or conceptions, because it accomplishes the intended purpose.
From this point onward, all the sūtras demonstrate the severing of the arising of doubt.
How does doubt arise?
If one practices giving without dwelling upon phenomena, how can it be considered practicing giving for the sake of the Buddha's enlightenment?
This [teaching] cuts through that doubt.

"Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of these marks? Subhūti replied, "No."
World-Honored One!
One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of physical marks. Why is this?
"The marks described by the Tathāgata are themselves no-marks. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All that has marks is entirely false speech."
"If one sees that all marks are no-marks, then one does not speak falsely.
Thus, by seeing that all marks are no-marks, one sees the Tathāgata.
The Commentary says:
The verse says:
Distinguishing the nature of the conditioned, One prevents the attainment of its establishment;
Because the three marks have distinct natures, That which is apart from them is the Tathāgata.
What is the meaning of this?

If one discriminates that the essence of the conditioned is the Tathāgata, taking the characteristics of the conditioned as primary, one perceives the Tathāgata through the accomplishment of those characteristics.

This is to prevent the attainment of the Tathāgata’s body through the accomplishment of those marks, as the sūtra states: "One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of marks. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is named the Unconditioned Dharma-body.
As the Sūtra says: "For what reason?
The characteristics spoken of by the Tathāgata are themselves non-characteristics."
The verse states: "Because the three marks are distinct entities, the Tathāgata is apart from them. The accomplishment of those marks is itself the non-accomplishment of marks. Why is this so?
Because the three marks are different from the essence of the Tathāgata, as the Sūtra says:
"The Buddha told Subhūti: 'Whatever has marks is all falsehood.'"
"If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one does not speak falsely.
Thus, by seeing that all marks are non-marks, one sees the Tathāgata. This sentence reveals that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are illusory.

The verse states, "Apart from those is the Tathāgata. This is shown because the three characteristics are absent there; because characteristics and the absence of characteristics are mutually relative; and because there, the distinct entities of arising, abiding, and ceasing cannot be found. This phrase clarifies that the essence of the Tathāgata is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

When a bodhisattva knows that the Tathāgata practices giving for the sake of the Buddha-enlightenment, that bodhisattva practices giving while not dwelling in any phenomena; it is by accomplishing such a severance of doubt.
From this point onward, the Venerable Subhūti gives rise to doubt and poses a question.
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:”
“World-Honored One!
Will there be sentient beings in the future age, in the final period, who, upon hearing such passages and verses of this sutra, will give rise to the perception of reality?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Do not say this: 'Will there be any sentient beings in the future age, in the final period, who, upon hearing such chapters and phrases of a sūtra as these, will give rise to the perception of reality?'"
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:

"In a future age, at the end of time, when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who maintain the precepts and cultivate merit and wisdom; they will be able to give rise to faith in the chapters and verses of this sūtra and regard them as true."
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:

"You should know that those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not practiced or made offerings under only one, two, three, four, or five buddhas; nor have they planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five buddhas."
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:

"Subhūti, those who have practiced and made offerings under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, and who have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, will be able to give rise to pure faith—even for a single thought-moment—upon hearing this sūtra."
The Tathāgata fully knows these sentient beings; the Tathāgata fully sees these sentient beings.
Subhūti! These bodhisattvas produce such an immeasurable accumulation of merit and take up such immeasurable merit.
Why is this? Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span.
Subhūti! These bodhisattvas have neither the perception of dharmas nor the perception of non-dharmas; they have no marks, yet they do not lack marks. Why is this?
Subhūti! If these bodhisattvas were to grasp at the marks of dharmas, they would be clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of dharmas, they are attached to the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, and the notion of a life-span.
Why is this? Subhūti!
One should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one fail to grasp at dharmas.

For this reason, the Tathāgata has always spoken of the Dharma-gate of the raft parable: these dharmas should be relinquished, yet it is not for the sake of relinquishing dharmas that they are relinquished.
The Commentary says:
What is the meaning of this?
Previously, based on the *pāramitās*, it was explained that one practices giving without dwelling [in it]; this explains the profound meaning of the cause.
Thus far, based on the Tathāgata’s non-conditioned essence, the profound meaning of the fruit has been explained.
If this is so, and people in the future evil age do not give rise to faith, why is it not said that [the teaching] is empty?
To sever that doubt, the Buddha answered this matter.
As the sutra says: "The Buddha told Subhūti:
'Do not speak thus... up to: it is not because of the dharma of relinquishment.'"
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
To proclaim the profound meaning of cause and effect In that time of the degenerate age,
Because it is not empty and possesses reality, the Bodhisattva is endowed with the three virtues.
What is the meaning of this?
In that evil age, because the Bodhisattva is fully possessed of the merit of upholding the precepts and wisdom, he is able to give rise to faith.
For this reason, it is called "teaching that is not in vain.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"Having cultivated precepts in the past, And having planted various roots of goodness,"
The precepts are perfected in all Buddhas, and their merit is also said to be complete.
As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:

'You should know that those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not practiced and made offerings under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas; nor have they planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas.'"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because they have already practiced and made offerings at the sites of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, and have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas."
This scriptural passage clarifies that the Buddhas of the past were fully endowed with the precepts and made offerings to those Buddhas, thereby planting various roots of goodness.
It is through such a sequence that they became fully endowed with the precepts and fully endowed with merit.
Furthermore, a verse says:
Those persons and phenomena are far removed from grasping at signs;
yet it is also said that one knows those signs, based on the distinctions among the eightfold and eightfold meanings.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because the meaning of *prajñā* is further explained as being uninterrupted.
What meaning is being explained?
This clarifies that because those bodhisattvas are free from the mark of a self (jīva-nimitta) and free from the mark of phenomena (dharma-nimitta), this meaning is taught in contrast to those marks.
As the verse states, "Based on the distinctions of the eightfold eightfold meanings," what does this mean?
Because there are four kinds of meanings based on the four kinds of characteristics of the person (pudgala),
and four kinds of meanings based on the four kinds of characteristics of phenomena (dharma);
therefore, based on these eight characteristics, there are eight distinct types of meaning.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
"The substance of the differentiated continuum persists without interruption until the end of life."
Furthermore, "further pursuing other paths" constitutes the four kinds of the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
What is the meaning of this?
It is to clarify the meaning of the mark of the life-principle (*jīvaka*).
What are these four? First, the mark of a self;
second, the mark of a sentient being;
Third is the mark of the life-principle;
fourth is the mark of the life-span.
As for the mark of the self, it is to perceive distinctions among the five aggregates and to regard each individual aggregate as the self.
Such false grasping is called the mark of self (*ātman*).
As for the mark of sentient beings (*sattva*), seeing the continuity of the body as uninterrupted is called the mark of sentient beings.
As for the mark of life (*jīva*), because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of a single retribution remains uninterrupted, it is called the mark of life.
The mark of a self-sustainer (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*) refers to the severance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), followed by rebirth within the six realms of existence;
this is called the mark of a self-sustainer. As the Sūtra says: "For what reason? Subhūti!"
"This is because these bodhisattvas no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span.
What about the dharma?
The verse says:
All things are empty and without substance; their actual existence cannot be expressed.
They are spoken of by relying on words and phrases; these are the four kinds of dharma-characteristics. What are these four?
First, the characteristic of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa);
second, the characteristic of non-phenomena (adharmalakṣaṇa);
third, the characteristic [itself] (lakṣaṇa).
The fourth is the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). What is the meaning of this?
Because all phenomena (*dharma*)—both the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehending (*grāhaka*)—do not exist, it is said that there is no characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Because there is no entity, that dharma is selfless; yet emptiness truly exists.

It is also not the case that it lacks the characteristic of existence, for while that emptiness is without substance, this [emptiness] cannot be said to be either existent or non-existent; therefore, it is called "without characteristics" (animitta), as it is spoken of by relying on conventional expression.
Speech is also not without characteristics.
Why is this? Because it is spoken by relying on the characteristics of speech within the realm where there is no speech.

Therefore, by relying on these eight kinds of distinct meanings and being free from the eight kinds of characteristics—namely, being free from the characteristic of a person (pudgala-nimitta) and being free from the characteristic of phenomena (dharma-nimitta)—one is said to possess wisdom.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas have no perception of dharmas, nor do they have a perception of non-dharmas;
they have no perception, nor do they have a perception of non-perception. Therefore, wisdom alone is sufficient.
For what reason is the merit of upholding the precepts further explained?
It is for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the distinctions among the characteristics of arising.
How is this demonstrated?
The verse says:
That person, relying on faith and reverence, gives rise to the perception of reality;
hearing sounds, they do not grasp them erroneously, but grasp them as they are correctly taught.
What is the meaning of this?
That person possesses the merit of upholding the precepts; by relying on faith and reverence, they are able to give rise to the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

It is for the sake of explaining this point that it is subsequently stated: "Those who, upon hearing such chapters and verses of the sūtra, give rise to pure faith even for a single thought-moment. Therefore, it is not only the Prajñāpāramitā that is being discussed.

Furthermore, those who possess wisdom do not grasp the meaning according to the sound; rather, they accord with the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and by correctly explaining it in this way, they are able to give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
For this reason, having explained this meaning, he next says: "Subhūti!..."
"One should not grasp at dharmas, yet it is not that one does not grasp at dharmas.
As for "one should not grasp at dharmas," one should not grasp at dharmas as they appear to the ear.
As for "it is not that one does not grasp at dharmas," one grasps them by correctly expounding in accordance with the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because that bodhisattva, upon hearing such words and phrases of the sūtra, gives rise to the perception of reality (bhūtārtha).
Furthermore, the sūtra says: "Subhūti!
The Tathāgata fully knows all these sentient beings; the Tathāgata fully sees all these sentient beings. What does this clarify?
The verse says:
The Buddha does not know by seeing the fruit; it is through the power of his vows and wisdom that he perceives directly.
Those who seek offerings and honor cannot speak of this.
What is the meaning of this?
Regarding those who uphold the precepts and so forth, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not know them by inferring from their results.
How, then, do they know them?
The verse says, "May the power of wisdom manifest and see.
Since it is sufficient for the Tathāgata to know all these sentient beings, why does he further say, "The Tathāgata sees all these sentient beings"?
If it were not stated that "the Tathāgata perceives all these sentient beings," one might suppose that the Tathāgata knows them through inferential cognition (anumāna-jñāna);
it is for fear that such a thought might arise.
If that is so, it would suffice merely to say, "The Tathāgata sees all these sentient beings"; why, then, does he further say, "The Tathāgata knows all these sentient beings"?
If it were not stated that "the Tathāgata fully knows all these sentient beings," one might suppose that the Tathāgata perceives them with the fleshly eye and so forth;
it is for the purpose of preventing such a misconception that this is said. Why is it stated thus?
Because there are two types of speech.
Furthermore, for what reason did the Tathāgata speak thus?
The verse states: "Those who seek offerings and honor are unable to speak [the truth]."
What is the meaning of this?

If someone desires to obtain offerings and respect, and praises themselves for possessing virtues such as the observance of precepts, that person would not be able to speak [of these virtues], because they know them only to themselves.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, thoroughly know what kind of persons they are and what their conduct is; therefore, those persons are unable to speak for themselves.
Furthermore, as for the statement, "These bodhisattvas produce such an immeasurable mass of merit and take up such immeasurable merit," what is the meaning of this?
"Arising" means it is the productive cause.
"Appropriation" means the sense of the fruit that perfumes and cultivates its own essence.
Furthermore, "Why is this so? [is asked].
"Subhūti! If these bodhisattvas were to grasp at the marks of dharmas, they would be clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. What is the meaning of this?

This is because there are only the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) without the manifestation of coarse afflictions, in order to demonstrate the absence of the view of self (*anātma-dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, regarding the scriptural statement: "For this reason, the Tathāgata has always taught the Dharma-gate of the raft simile: 'These dharmas should be relinquished; do not cling even to these dharmas,'" what is the sequential logic here?
The verse says:
He does not abide in conformity, but realizes wisdom within the Dharma;
just as a person abandons a boat or raft, so too is the meaning within the Dharma.
What is the meaning of this?

It indicates that within the teachings of the sūtras and other dharmas, realized wisdom does not abide; because one attains realized wisdom, one relinquishes those dharmas, just as one abandons a raft upon reaching the further shore.
"Conformity" means conforming to that dharma of realized wisdom.
That dharma should be grasped, just as one who has not yet reached the far shore takes up a raft.
From this point onward, what meaning is being explained?
This is to prevent further doubt.
What is this further doubt?
It is the doubt that arose from the previous statement that one cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of physical marks.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata does not receive his name by virtue of conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
If this is so, how is it that Śākyamuni Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and is designated as a "Buddha"?
What is the teaching of the Dharma?
This is called the doubt regarding difference; it is for the purpose of severing this doubt. How is doubt severed?
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the venerable Subhūti: 'Subhūti!'"
"What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?"

Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can teach."
Why is this? All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are neither to be grasped nor to be spoken; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas. Why is this?
"All noble ones receive their names from the dharma of non-action.
The Commentary says:
For this reason, Śākyamuni Buddha is not a Buddha, nor does he preach the Dharma.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
The response-body and transformation-body are not the true Buddha, Nor are they the speakers of the Dharma.
The teaching of the Dharma is non-dual and free from grasping; it is without speech and transcends verbal characteristics.
What is the meaning of this?
There are three kinds of Buddhas:
First is the Dharma-body Buddha;
second is the Reward-body Buddha;
third is the Transformation-body Buddha.
Furthermore, as for the one named Śākyamuni who is called a Buddha, this is a transformation Buddha; this Buddha did not realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor did he preach the Dharma.

As the Sūtra says: "There is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach. If this is so, for what reason does the Sūtra say: "Why is that?"?
Regarding such statements as, "All that the Tathāgata has taught cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken," some people slanderously claim:
"The Tathāgata never teaches the Dharma at all."
To preclude this [misconception], the verse states: "The manifested and transformational [bodies] are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma.

Regarding the line, "In the teaching of the Dharma, there is no dualistic grasping; there is no speaking, as it is free from the characteristics of words," this means that the listener does not grasp at the Dharma, nor do they grasp at what is non-Dharma.
The speaker also does not speak dualistically, because of the nature of phenomena and non-phenomena. Why is this?
Those phenomena are neither phenomena nor non-phenomena; in what sense, then, are they spoken of?
This is explained according to the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
It is "not dharmas" because all dharmas lack intrinsic nature and characteristics.
It is "not non-dharmas" because that *tathatā* exists as a reality, being characterized by the absence of self (*anātman*).
Why is it that one speaks only of verbal expression and not of realization?
Because where there is verbal expression, the meaning of realization is thereby established;
if one has not realized it, one cannot speak of it.
As the sutra says: "For what reason?
All noble ones (ārya) are designated by the name 'unconditioned dharma' (asaṃskṛtadharma).
What meaning does this sentence clarify?
That dharma is explained as the cause.

Why is this? All noble ones (ārya) receive their names based on the purity of the dharma of true thusness (tathatā), for they receive their names by virtue of the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
For this reason, those noble ones speak of that unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Furthermore, for what reason?
Just as that dharma realized by those noble ones cannot be described in such a way, how much less can it be grasped in such a manner!
Why is this? Because those dharmas are remote from the characteristics of language and are not things that can be expressed in speech.
Why, then, does it not merely speak of the Buddha, but rather speaks of all noble ones (*ārya*)?
Because all noble ones (ārya) receive their names based on the purity of suchness (tathatā), they are thus endowed with complete purity and the purity of suchness.
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
What do you think, Subhūti?
If one were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Is the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family not great? Subhūti replied:
"Very much so, Blessed One! Very much so."
Sugata! Those sons and daughters of good family will acquire exceedingly great merit. Why is that?
“World-Honored One!
This accumulation of merit is indeed not an accumulation of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of an ‘accumulation of merit, accumulation of merit. The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! If a good man or a good woman were to take seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift;

yet if another were to receive, uphold, or even recite as little as a four-line verse from this sutra and explain it for others, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former, being immeasurable and incalculable.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
All the dharmas of the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas emerge from this sūtra; all the Tathāgatas of all Buddhas are born from this sūtra.
“Subhūti! What is called ‘Buddha-dharma,’ Buddha-dharma is not Buddha-dharma; it is designated as ‘Buddha-dharma.
The Commentary says:
This explanation of the analogy for comparing superior merit demonstrates what meaning?
It shows that although phenomena are ungraspable and inexpressible, they are not empty.
The verse says:
Upholding the Dharma and expounding it are not in vain regarding merit;
yet merit alone does not lead to enlightenment—it is these two that can lead to enlightenment.
Why is it said, "World-Honored One!
This mass of merit is itself no mass of merit"?
The verse states: "Merit does not lead to Bodhi; these two can lead to Bodhi."
What is the meaning of this?
That merit does not lead to great enlightenment, whereas these two can lead to great enlightenment. What are the two?
The first is upholding;
the second is expounding.
This is because the sutra states: "Uphold [even] as little as a four-line verse, and explain it for others."
Why is it called a "mass of merit" (*puṇyaskandha*)?
There are two meanings of "mass": first, the meaning of accumulation; [second, the meaning of a collection].
Second is the sense of "progressing toward.
Just as a person carrying a heavy load is said to have a "burden," so too this accumulation of merit is called a "heap" (rāśi) because it possesses the quality of being accumulated.
Because one cannot progress toward enlightenment [by means of it], it is called a non-heap of merit.
These two, however, can lead to great enlightenment; therefore, among those merits, this merit is superior.
How can these two attain great enlightenment?
As the sutra says: "For what reason, Subhūti?"
This is because "the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas emerges from this sutra, and all Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are born from this sutra."
Why is it said that "the bodhi-dharmas of all Buddhas all emerge from this sutra"?
Why is it said that "all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are all born from this sutra"?
The verse says:
Regarding reality, it is the cause of manifestation; it is also the cause for the arising of others.
Only the qualities of the Buddhas constitute the foremost substance through the perfection of merit.
What is the meaning of this?
Awakening (bodhi) is termed the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and its essence is truly unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Therefore, with respect to that Dharma-body, these two [causes] can function as causes of manifestation (vyañjanahetu), but cannot function as causes of production (janakahetu).
As for the others, they receive retribution characterized by the marks and signs of physical adornment.

Regarding the marks and signs of the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the Buddha serves as their generative cause (*janakahetu*) because he can act as the cause for awakening; therefore, it is called a "cause. This is to show that among all merits, this particular merit is superior.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "For what reason? Subhūti!
Because everything arises from this sūtra."
How is this meaning established?
The verse states: "Only the Buddha-dharmas alone constitute the supreme essence of merit.
Thus [the Buddha said], "Subhūti!..."

Regarding the statement, "What is called 'Buddha-dharma,' Buddha-dharma is not Buddha-dharma": those various Buddha-dharmas cannot be attained by others; for this reason, those Buddha-dharmas are named "Buddha-dharma."
Therefore, it is said: "Exclusively the qualities of the Buddhas.

This refers to the meaning of the foremost unique [attribute], because it can act as the cause for the foremost dharma; thus, among all merits, this merit is supreme, and in this way, it establishes a vastness of merit.
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Could a stream-enterer have this thought:
'Have I attained the fruit of stream-entry?'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
"In truth, there is no dharma named 'srotāpanna.
One who does not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas is called a srotāpanna.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a sakṛdāgāmin have such a thought as this:”
"Have I attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin? Subhūti replied, "No."
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Truly there is no dharma named "once-returner," yet it is designated as "once-returner."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can an Anāgāmin form such a thought as this:”
"Have I attained the fruit of anāgāmin? Subhūti replied, "No."
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Truly there is no dharma named "Anāgāmin"; it is merely designated as "Anāgāmin."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can an Arhat form such a thought as this:..."
"Have I attained arhatship? Subhūti replied, "No."
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Truly, there is no dharma that can be called an Arhat.
"Bhagavān! If an Arhat were to have this thought:
'I have attained Arhatship.'"
"Then one would be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
World-Honored One!
The Buddha has declared that I am foremost among those who have attained the samādhi of non-contention; the World-Honored One has declared that I am an arhat free from desire."
"Bhagavān! I do not entertain the thought:
'I am a desire-free arhat.'"
“World-Honored One!
If I were to have this thought:
‘I have attained arhatship.’”
The World-Honored One does not say that I am foremost in the practice of non-contention.
Because Subhūti truly has no practice, he is named Subhūti, the one of non-contention, the one whose practice is non-contention.
The Commentary states:
It was previously explained that the noble ones obtain their designation through unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). For this reason, those dharmas cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed.
If noble ones such as the *srotāpanna* and others grasp their own respective fruits, how can it be said that those dharmas are ungraspable?
Since they are realized as they are and explained as they are, how can they be established as inexpressible?
The following scriptural passage is intended to sever this doubt, establishing that those dharmas are neither graspable nor expressible.
The verse says:
Neither graspable nor expressible, Because their own fruit is not grasped.
Relying on that Subhūti, he speaks of being free from the two kinds of hindrances.
What is the meaning of this?
Because the Noble One is designated by means of unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharma), he does not grasp at a single dharma.
"Non-appropriation" means not appropriating the objects of the six sense-fields.
For this reason, it is called non-appropriation.
"Flowing against the current" is as stated in the Sūtra: "Not entering into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena—this is called a srotāpanna."
Up to and including the Arhat, not a single dharma is grasped; for this reason, they are called Arhats.
Nevertheless, it is not that the Noble Ones do not grasp unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), for they do grasp their own fruition.
If a noble one were to give rise to such a thought as,
"I am able to attain the fruit," they would then be attached to a self; what is the meaning of this?
Because these are afflictions that involve propelling [one into rebirth], not afflictions of active conduct. Why is this?
At the time of realization, one is free from afflictions such as grasping at a self; therefore, no such thought arises:
"I am able to attain the fruit.
For what reason does the Venerable Subhūti praise himself as having received the prediction and testify to the attainment of the fruit through his own person?
It is for the sake of generating faith in that meaning.
For what reason is only the practice of non-contention (araṇā) taught?
It is to clarify its superior merit and to engender deep faith.
Why is it said, "Because Subhūti has in reality nothing to practice, he is named Subhūti of Non-contention, the one whose practice is non-contention"?
The verse says: "Relying on that Subhūti, he spoke of being free from the two kinds of obscurations. As for these two kinds of obscurations:
the first is the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); [the second is the obscuration of knowables].
The second is the obstacle to samādhi.
Because one is free from these two obstacles, it is said that there is "no sphere of activity.
For this reason, it is called the "two kinds of contention."
Because one is free from those two kinds of hindrances, it is called "non-contention" (*araṇā*) and the "practice of non-contention.
The Sūtra says:
"The Buddha addressed Subhūti:"
"What do you think?
When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, did he obtain the dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly attained nothing at all as 'anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi' regarding the Dharma."
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, there is a doubt:
Śākyamuni Tathāgata received the Dharma from Dīpaṃkara Buddha in the past, and that Buddha preached the Dharma for this Buddha.
If this is so, why are those dharmas unspeakable and ungraspable?
To sever this doubt, it is said that in the Buddha’s realm there is no dharma that can be grasped.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
“No, World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly attained nothing at all regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
For what reason is it said thus?
The verse states:
Regarding the words of Dīpaṃkara, the Buddha did not grasp at the wisdom of ultimate reality.
By means of this true meaning, that teaching of non-appropriation is established.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he did not appropriate the dharma taught through words as a realization.
For this reason, it is shown that the realized wisdom (pratyātmajñāna) is ineffable and ungraspable.
As the verse states: "By means of this true meaning, that which is without grasping is established as being beyond expression."
Furthermore, if the name "unconditioned dharma" is applied to the dharmas of the sages, then these dharmas cannot be grasped and cannot be described;
how then do the bodhisattvas grasp the adornment of the pure buddha-fields?
How is it that he experiences the retribution of pleasure, yet the Buddha assumes for himself the body of a Dharma King?
And how is it that other beings in the world also take him to be the body of a Dharma King?
The following scriptural passage is intended to sever this doubt.
The Sūtra says:
"The Buddha told Subhūti:
'If a bodhisattva were to speak thus:'"
"To adorn the Buddha-lands"—
those bodhisattvas speak untruthfully. Why is this?
Subhūti! That which the Tathāgata calls the adornment of Buddha-fields is in fact no adornment; it is merely designated as the "adornment of Buddha-fields. Therefore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way, yet without abiding anywhere. They should not give rise to the mind by abiding in forms;
they should not give rise to the mind by abiding in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. They should give rise to that mind without abiding in anything at all.
"Subhūti! It is as if, for example, there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains. Subhūti!"
"What do you think? Is this body great? Subhūti replied:
"Extremely great,
World-Honored One! Why is this?"
"The Buddha said that what is not a body is called the 'great body.
That body is no-body; it is for this reason it is called the 'great body. The Treatise says:
This meaning should be understood in this way. How is it known?
The verse says:
When wisdom practices the penetration of *vijñapti-mātra*, one thus takes hold of a pure land;
it is not a physical form, but the primary essence, and not a decoration, but the intention of adornment.
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddhas have no concern for the adornment of their lands;
it is only through the thorough penetration of the habitual consciousness of the true wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgatas that those lands are perceived, and therefore they cannot be grasped.
If a person grasps at the physical characteristics of that buddha-field and says,
"I have accomplished a pure buddha-field," they speak untruthfully.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "For what reason?
Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the adornment of the Buddha-fields is in fact no adornment; it is merely designated as 'the adornment of the Buddha-fields.'"
Why is it stated thus? The verse says:
"The primary essence is not form; it is not the intention of adornment. There are two kinds of adornment: [physical adornment and mental adornment].
The first is the mark of form, and the second is the mark of the ultimate truth; therefore, it is said that there is no adornment.
Furthermore, that which does not adorn the Buddha-land has no marks of form; thus, it is not adorned.
Thus, the absence of adornment is itself the supreme adornment. Why is this?
Because it is adorned by the accomplishment of all meritorious qualities.

If a person discriminates the Buddha-land as having conditioned characteristics and says, "I shall accomplish a pure Buddha-land," that bodhisattva dwells within the spheres of form and so forth and gives rise to such a mind. To prevent this, as the sutra says: "Therefore, Subhūti!"
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind while dwelling nowhere. They should not dwell on forms when giving rise to the mind;
they should not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas when giving rise to the mind; they should give rise to that mind while dwelling in nothing at all. Thus it is said.
Preface: "How does one receive the retribution of bliss? How does the Buddha assume the body of the Dharma King himself?
And how do others in the world likewise take on that very body of the Dharma King?"
To eliminate this doubt, it is taught that the Buddha-body which experiences the retribution of bliss is identical to that King of Mountains, Sumeru, by virtue of the principle of reflected images.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
Like the king of mountains, he has no grasping; his reception of retribution is likewise so.
This is because he is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What is the meaning of this?
Just as the King of Mountains, Sumeru, is called "Great" because its power is lofty and far-reaching, yet it does not grasp at the essence of that mountain king,
thinking, "I am the king of mountains," for it is free from discrimination.

The Buddha who receives the retribution of bliss is also like this: because he has attained the essence of the unsurpassed Dharma King, he is called "Great," yet he does not grasp at that essence of the Dharma King, thinking, "I am the Dharma King."
Because it is non-conceptual. Why is it non-conceptual?
Because it is non-conceptual.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "For what reason?
The Buddha has taught that what is not a body is called the 'great body.
That body is no-body; it is for this reason called the 'great body.'"
Why is it said thus? The verse states:
"Because it is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

That Buddha-body which experiences the retribution of bliss is free from all outflows. If it were such [as a mere non-entity], it would not be a thing; yet if it were such, it is called a thing, because it possesses only a pure body and is far removed from conditioned phenomena.
For this reason, there truly exists a self-substance (*ātman*), because it abides without depending on other conditions.
