The scripture says:
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River— what do you think?”
"Would these grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers be many? Subhūti replied, "Very many."
“World-Honored One!
Even the Ganges Rivers alone are already countless, let alone their sands!
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! I now tell you this in truth:

if there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures, filled as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and gave them as gifts to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas."
Subhūti, what do you think?
Would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Subhūti said: "Very much, World-Honored One!"
"That son or daughter of good family will acquire much more merit.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If one were to fill as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, and if a son or daughter of good family were instead to take up even a four-line verse from this Dharma-gate and explain it to others, the merit of the latter would surpass the former by immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* amounts."
The Commentary says:
Previously, many analogies for great merit were already explained; why are they stated again here?
The verse says:
By explaining the distinctions among many meanings, one also achieves a superior comparison;
since the subsequent merit exceeds the former, I shall again state a superior analogy.
What is the meaning of this?
Previously, the analogy of three thousandfold world systems was taught to clarify the vastness of merit; now, it is taught again with reference to immeasurable three thousandfold world systems.
For what reason was this analogy not taught first?
This is for the purpose of gradually transforming sentient beings so that they may give rise to faith in the sublime and wondrous meaning.

Furthermore, since it had not previously been revealed by what superior merits one can attain great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), these metaphors are used to establish those merits; therefore, these superior metaphors are stated again.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this Dharma-gate is taught—even if only as much as a four-line verse—one should know that this place should be honored by all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha; how much more so for one who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite this entire sūtra."
Subhūti! You should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme and foremost rare and wonderful Dharma.
Wherever this sutra resides, there is a Buddha; one should honor it as if it were the Buddha himself.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this Dharma-gate be named?”
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This Dharma-door is named 'Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā'; by this name you should receive and uphold it."
Why is this? Subhūti,
that which the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is, in fact, not the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma?
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One,
there is no dharma taught by the Tathāgata."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many?”
Subhūti said: “Those atoms would be very numerous,
World-Honored One!”
"Why is that? Subhūti! These atoms, the Tathāgata has said, are not atoms; they are called 'atoms'."
"The Tathāgata speaks of the world as not a world; it is merely named 'the world. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
“The Tathāgata says that the thirty-two marks of a great man are themselves non-marks; they are called the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The Commentary asks:
How are those supreme merits accomplished?
The verse says:
One honors two states; through cultivation, one realizes the Great Essence.
Through that cultivation, one deals with afflictions; herein, one subdues defilement while gathering merit.

What is the meaning of this? "Honoring two locations" refers to: first, the location where it is taught; wherever this sutra is preached, one generates a sense of respect and wonder toward that place.

Second, the person who teaches it; whoever is able to receive, uphold, and preach it, one honors them because of their reverence for the sutra and its treatises. This is not like the case of the seven precious jewels, which may be given away anywhere or by anyone; such [reverence] gives rise to profound respect because this Dharma-gate serves as the supreme cause for the realization-dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
As the Sūtra says: "Subhūti said:
'World-Honored One!
Because the Tathāgata has no Dharma that he teaches. What is the meaning of this?"
There is not a single dharma that is taught by the Tathāgata alone and not taught by other Buddhas.
The merit of giving precious jewels is a cause for defiled afflictions, because it can bring about the occurrence of afflictions.
This cause is shown because it demonstrates the distancing from the causes of affliction; therefore, the analogy of the atoms of the earth is taught. As the Sūtra says:
“Subhūti, these atoms, which the Tathāgata has preached, are not atoms; they are called ‘atoms.’”
"The Tathāgata speaks of the world as not being a world; it is merely called 'the world. Why is this said?

Those atoms are not the substance of afflictions such as greed; for this reason, they are termed "earth-atoms. Therefore, that world is not a realm that serves as the cause for the defilement of afflictions; thus, it is called "the world."
What does this clarify?

That merit is the cause for the defilement of the dust of afflictions; therefore, among external indeterminate objects, that merit serves as a proximate cause for the roots of goodness. How much more so, since this merit can bring about the awakening of a Buddha, and because it is superior among the merits that accomplish the marks of a Great Man.
Therefore, upholding and expounding this Dharma-gate brings about the attainment of Buddha-enlightenment, and its merit surpasses that [of other deeds]. Why is this?
Because those marks are not marks with respect to Buddha-enlightenment, for they are not the Dharma-body.
Therefore, it is said that the marks of a Great Man [are taught] because of those very marks.
This merit derived from upholding and explaining [the teachings] can bring about the awakening of a Buddha; for that reason, those [marks] are not superior.
Furthermore, that merit is capable of surpassing the merit derived from precious jewels and the like; how much more so this merit? Therefore, this merit is both most proximate and most supreme.
Thus, among the merits of those [practices] such as giving (*dāna*), this merit is the most supreme; having been established in this way, the Sūtra says:
“The Buddha said:”
“Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who were to give away their lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;

yet if another person, from within this Dharma-gate, were to even receive and uphold a four-line verse or the like and explain it to others, the merit of the latter would be far greater—immeasurable and incalculable.”

At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; with tears streaming down his face in sorrowful weeping, he wiped away his tears and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, O Bhagavān!"
"How rare, Sugata!
That the Buddha has preached such a profound Dharma-gate; from my past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard such a Dharma-gate."
"Why is that? Subhūti, the Buddha says that 'prajñāpāramitā' is indeed not prajñāpāramitā."
“World-Honored One!
If there should be anyone who hears this sutra and, with pure faith, gives rise to the mark of reality, you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.”
“World-Honored One!
This true mark is in fact no mark; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name ‘true mark,’ ‘true mark.
World-Honored One!”
That I have now heard such a Dharma-gate and am able to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult;
however, if there should be sentient beings in future ages who hear this Dharma-gate and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, those people would be the most rare and extraordinary of all.
Why is this? Because this person has no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span. Why is this?
The mark of a self is itself no-mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no-marks. Why is this?
Because one who is free from all marks is called a Buddha.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is.
If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is exceedingly rare.”
Why is this? Subhūti,
that which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not, in fact, a foremost pāramitā.
"The Tathāgata speaks of the foremost *pāramitā*; those immeasurable Buddhas also speak of this *pāramitā*, and it is therefore called the foremost *pāramitā*.
The Commentary states:
From here on in the sutra text, it is further clarified that among those merits, this merit is superior.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
"A body that undergoes suffering is superior to that [other body]; it is rare and possesses the highest significance."
That shore of wisdom is difficult to measure, and it is not like other dharmas.
Firm and substantial, it understands the profound meaning;
it surpasses other sūtras in its great cause and purity, being the most excellent merit among all merits.
What is the meaning of these two verses?
They state that the renunciation of body and life is more significant than the renunciation of material wealth, precious jewels, and the like.
Since such [renunciation] results in the merit of the retribution of immeasurable lives, this merit surpasses that other merit.
Why is this? Because he has already relinquished the suffering of body and mind by sacrificing his own life, how much more so would he do so for the sake of the Dharma?
Recalling that physical suffering, the wise Subhūti, out of his profound reverence for the Dharma, wept and shed tears.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "At that time, Subhūti, upon hearing this discourse on the Dharma, deeply understood its meaning and intent, and wept with tears of sorrow.
Therefore, this Dharma-gate is rare and marvelous.
Why is this? Although the Venerable Subhūti possesses the eye of wisdom, he has never before heard such a thing; therefore, it is rare.
As the sutra says: "Since I first attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard such a Dharma-gate."
Furthermore, this dharma-gate is supreme because it is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
How is this established?
By virtue of the aforementioned meaning.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "For what reason?
Subhūti, that which the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is indeed not the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Why is it said thus? Because it is the shore of that wisdom.
Since no person can measure that shore of wisdom, it is therefore not a *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, this dharma-gate is not the same [as others].
Why is this? Because within it, there is the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
The remainder are not the true nature, because apart from the Buddha-dharma, there is no reality elsewhere;
this is because in those other places, such things have never existed and faith has never been produced. For this reason.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "World-Honored One!
If there should be anyone who hears this sūtra and their faith becomes pure, then the true mark will arise; you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit."
Furthermore, this Dharma-gate is solid, profound, and subtle.
Why is this? Because by receiving, upholding, contemplating, and practicing this sutra, one does not give rise to the notion of "self" and so forth.
Furthermore, the non-arising of the notion of "self" and so forth demonstrates the unerring characteristic of the objective sphere (*grāhya-viṣaya*).
That the notion of "self" and so forth is itself no-characteristic demonstrates the unerring characteristic of the subjective sphere (*grāhaka-viṣaya*).
These two clarify the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena due to the wisdom of non-self.
This sequence is as stated in the Sūtra: "For what reason?
Because this person lacks the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span."
Why is this? The mark of a self is itself no-mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no-marks. Why is this?
Because it is said that "to be free from all these marks is what is called the Buddhas," the Tathāgata spoke this meaning to Subhūti.

To be "startled" means to give rise to fear where there is no occasion for it; thus it is called "startled. It is so called because it is censurable, just as it is when one practices a path that is not the true way.
"Terrified" (*bhīta*) refers to the essential nature of the mind being afraid.
Because it gives rise to a state that cannot sever doubt, "fearful" (*bhīru*) refers to being consistently afraid.
Since the mind ultimately falls into a state of alarm and dread, one should distance oneself from that place.
As the sutra says: "without alarm, without terror, and without fear.
Furthermore, this dharma-gate excels other sūtras, as the sutra asks:
"For what reason, Subhūti?"
This is because the Tathāgata has said, "The foremost pāramitā is not the foremost pāramitā.
Furthermore, this dharma-gate is called the Great Cause, as the sūtra says, "That which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā..."
Furthermore, this dharma-gate is called "pure" because it is taught by immeasurable Buddhas.
As the sutra states: "Those immeasurable Buddhas also teach the pāramitās; these are called the foremost pāramitās."
Those precious treasures, such as sandalwood and the like, do not possess such merit; therefore, among those merits, this merit is superior. Having established this, the treatise states:
From here on, the scriptural text further serves to eliminate doubts.
What is doubt? Previously it was said that because one abandons the body, which is the fruit of bodily suffering, that merit is inferior.

If that is so, then since the various bodhisattva practices involve the performance of asceticism and those ascetic acts are themselves the fruit of suffering, why would this dharma-gate not also result in the fruit of suffering?
In order to sever this doubt,
the Sūtra says: “Subhūti!...”
When the Tathāgata speaks of the perfection of patience, it is not a perfection of patience.
Why is this so, Subhūti?

When I was formerly cut and mangled limb by limb by King Kali, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span; there was neither form nor the absence of form.
Why is this? Subhūti!
When my limbs were being severed joint by joint in the past, if there had been in me any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.

Subhūti! Furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi practicing patience; during all those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while remaining detached from all marks. Why is this?
If the mind dwells anywhere, it is not truly dwelling.

One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere; therefore, the Buddha says that the Bodhisattva’s mind does not dwell on forms when practicing giving.
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
The marks of all sentient beings are themselves non-marks. Why is this?
"The Tathāgata says that all sentient beings are, in fact, not sentient beings.
The Commentary asks:
What meaning does this demonstrate?
The verse says:
One who is able to endure ascetic practices, for such practices possess goodness, their merit is immeasurable; this is the most supreme meaning.
Free from the notions of self and ill-will, Truly without suffering or affliction,
Sharing joy and possessing loving-kindness and compassion— Such are the fruits of ascetic practice.
What is the meaning of these two verses?
Although these ascetic practices are similar to their bitter fruits, one does not grow weary of them, for they are called the foremost because of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
The term "the other shore" (pāra) has two meanings:
first, it is the essence of the pure roots of goodness of the *pāramitās*;
second, the merit of the "other shore" is immeasurable.
As it says in the Sūtra: "It is not a pāramitā.
That which is not a pāramitā is so called because no one knows its shore of merit.
By saying it is not a pāramitā, it is therefore for the sake of attaining the foremost dharma.
This ascetic practice is superior to that sacrifice of the body, let alone because it is free from the marks of selfhood and ill-will.
Furthermore, this practice is without suffering; not only is it without suffering, but it possesses joy, for it is endowed with loving-kindness and compassion.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "At that time, I had no perception of a self, up to and including no perception of marks, nor even the absence of marks.
This is stated because [the Buddha] was in association with a mind of loving-kindness and compassion. Thus it is explained.

If there are bodhisattvas who do not depart from the notion of a self and so forth, those bodhisattvas perceive ascetic practices as suffering and also wish to abandon the mind of enlightenment; it is for their sake that this is taught.
As the Sūtra states: "Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should remain detached from all marks," and so forth.
What does this clarify?
Those who have not yet given rise to the supreme bodhicitta possess such faults; to prevent these faults, the verse says:
"In order to not abandon the mind, one should give rise to it, practice it, and remain steadfast."
For the sake of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), one practices that mind capable of learning.
What is the meaning of this?
With what kind of mental state does one give rise to the aspect of practice and cultivate it?
Why is it that this mind does not abandon its characteristics?
The verse states: "For the sake of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), one cultivates that mind capable of learning.
Furthermore, as for the mind of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-citta), it is because one has already entered the first stage (prathamā bhūmi) and attained the perfection of patience.
This is called the non-abiding mind, as the sutra states:
"Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while remaining detached from all signs."
Why is this? It is because it demonstrates the meaning of not dwelling in the arising of the mind.
If the mind dwells in dharmas such as form, that mind does not dwell in the Buddha’s bodhi; this clarifies that non-dwelling mental activity constitutes the practice of giving.

This scriptural passage explains the skillful means of initiating practice with a mind that does not dwell [on objects], because the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) subsumes all six perfections.
How is it that one practices for the benefit of sentient beings yet is not said to "dwell" in the affairs of sentient beings?
To sever this doubt, it is as the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!
A bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner."
What does this clarify?
The verse says:
One should recognize that practicing for the benefit of sentient beings is the cause in this manner.
One should also know that sentient beings and the characteristics of phenomena are far removed [from reality].
What is the meaning of this?
It is because benefit is the essence of the cause.
That practitioner benefits sentient beings because they do not grasp at the characteristic of a "sentient being.
What constitutes the matter of a sentient being?
The verse says:
The conventional designation and the aggregates— The Tathāgata is free from those characteristics;
The Buddhas do not possess these two, Because they perceive the true Dharma.
What is the meaning of this statement?
This is because of the entities of names, signs, sentient beings, and the aggregates.
How does that practitioner distance themselves from the phenomena of sentient beings?
It is because those very characteristics of names and signs are non-characteristics, as they lack any substantial reality.
For this reason, sentient beings are not [truly] sentient beings.
By what dharma? It is said that the five aggregates are called "sentient beings."
Those five aggregates have no essence of a sentient being because they lack substantial reality.
In this way, one clarifies the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) and the selflessness of persons (pudgalanairātmya). Why is this?

Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are far removed from all marks (*nimitta*), this phrase clarifies that those two marks are unreal. As the verse says: "The Tathāgata is free from those marks; the Buddhas possess neither of those two," because they perceive the true Dharma.
What is the meaning of this statement?
If those two were substantially existent, then the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, would possess those two characteristics. Why is that?
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, see according to reality.
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
The Tathāgata speaks truth, speaks reality, speaks as it is, and does not speak otherwise. Subhūti,
regarding the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata and the Dharma taught by him, there is neither reality nor falsehood.
The Commentary says:
Herein, there may be doubt that within the realization of the fruit (phala) there is no path; how then can that [path] act as a cause for the fruit?
To sever this doubt, it is as the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks reality, one who speaks as it is, and one who does not speak otherwise.
What meaning do these four phrases express?
The verse says:
Although the fruit does not abide in the path, the path can nonetheless serve as its cause;
by virtue of the true speech of all Buddhas, that wisdom is of four kinds.
What is the meaning of this?
There are four kinds of objects; therefore, the Tathāgata has four kinds of true speech.
What are these four kinds?
The verse says:
Because they speak of true wisdom and the Hīnayāna,
the Mahāyāna dharma, and all prophecies, without speaking falsely.
What does this clarify?

It means that by means of the Tathāgata’s true wisdom, he does not speak falsely regarding the Buddha’s bodhi, nor does he speak falsely regarding the matters of the Hīnayāna, the Mahāyāna, or the bestowal of predictions; this is because these constitute the four objects [of his discourse].
The four phrases are explained in sequence, as the Sūtra states:
"Subhūti, the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks reality, one who speaks according to suchness, and one who does not speak otherwise."
One does not falsely teach the Hīnayāna because one teaches that the Truth of Suffering and so forth in the Hīnayāna are indeed truths.
One does not falsely teach the Mahāyāna because one teaches the *tathatā* (suchness) of the selflessness of phenomena; for suchness is precisely suchness itself.
He does not speak falsely regarding the bestowal of prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), because he bestows prophecies concerning all that is past, future, and present.
He speaks in accordance with the true meaning, for he is without error.
The Sūtra further states: "Subhūti!
The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata and the Dharma taught by him are neither real nor false.
For what reason is this said?
The verse says:
In accordance with that true wisdom, it is said to be neither unreal nor real;
like taking realization based on hearing sounds, such teachings are spoken as an antidote.
What is the meaning of this?
Regarding the teachings expounded by all Buddhas, these teachings cannot themselves attain that Dharma which is to be realized.
Nevertheless, because they accord with the truth, the teachings expounded serve as the means by which that realized Dharma is attained.
Why is this? Because the sounds as they are heard do not possess such meanings, they are therefore without reality.
Since these spoken teachings accord with the Dharma of realization, there is no falsehood therein.
If that is so, why does it say "the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata" and "the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata"?
It is because these are spoken in reliance upon words and phrases.
Why, then, did the Tathāgata previously state that the Tathāgata is one who speaks truthfully, yet further say that the Dharma he teaches is neither real nor false?
The verse says: "Just as one takes realization upon hearing the sound, the antidote is taught in this way.
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
For example, it is as if a person enters the darkness and sees nothing at all.
If a bodhisattva dwells upon phenomena while practicing giving, it is just like this.
Subhūti, it is as if a person with eyes, when the night has ended and the light of the sun shines forth, sees various forms.
"If it is so for a Bodhisattva who practices giving while not dwelling on phenomena, it is likewise in this case.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, there is a doubt: if a Sage is named after the unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness), and that *tathatā* exists at all times and in all places, how can one attain the Buddha's *bodhi* by means of a mind that does not dwell? If it were [merely] not dwelling, it would not be [the attainment of] *bodhi*.
If true suchness exists truly at all times and in all places, why is it that some people are able to attain it while others are not?
To sever this doubt, the metaphors of entering darkness and so forth are taught.
What does this clarify?
The verse says:
Time and place exist substantially, yet true suchness is not attained.
Those without wisdom abide in phenomena; others, possessing wisdom, attain [liberation].
What is the meaning of this?
"At all times" refers to the past, present, and future.
"All places" refers to the three periods of time.
If sentient beings truly possess the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, why do they not attain it?
The verse states: "Because of dwelling in dharmas due to a lack of wisdom."
That lack of wisdom arises because the mind abides in phenomena.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because it is not pure.
Because the mind of the wise does not dwell upon phenomena, they are thus able to attain it.
For this reason, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are designated by the name "Pure True Suchness"; therefore, by dwelling upon the mind, one cannot attain the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Furthermore, what meaning does this analogy clarify?
The verse says:
Darkness and light represent ignorance and lack of wisdom; The luminous one is like one who possesses wisdom.
The antidote and the counter-factors, through which the state of cessation is attained, are thus.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because the analogy of darkness and light corresponds to the nature of these phenomena.
"Darkness" manifests the absence of wisdom; "the radiance of the sun" manifests the presence of wisdom.
What is the meaning of "one who has eyes"?
A verse states: "The antidote and the object to be countered, as well as the attainment and the cessation of phenomena, are thus."
In this successive order, "one who has eyes" is like the remedial dharmas;
"the night having ended" is like the ending of the darkness that is to be remedied.
"Those who are illuminated by the light of the sun" refers to the manifestation of the dharmas capable of healing.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person who enters darkness; then he sees nothing," and so forth.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Subhūti!

If there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this Dharma-gate, then the Tathāgata, with his Buddha-wisdom, fully knows these people, fully sees these people, and fully awakens to these people; they shall all achieve an immeasurable and boundless mass of merit."

Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who, in the first part of the day, gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and in the middle part of the day, again gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and in the latter part of the day, again gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

Those who delight in inferior teachings will be unable to accept, uphold, read, recite, practice, or explain this sutra to others.

It is impossible for anyone who holds views of a self, views of a sentient being, views of a person, or views of a life-span to accept, uphold, read, recite, practice, or explain this Dharma-gate to others.

Subhūti! Wherever this sutra may be found, it should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras. You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; everyone should pay homage, circumambulate it with reverence, and scatter various flowers and incense upon that spot.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sūtra, they will be held in contempt by others. Why is this?

If this person’s karmic offenses from previous lives were such that they should have fallen into the evil realms, because they are now treated with contempt by others in this life, those karmic offenses from previous lives will be extinguished, and they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti! I recall that in the past, during immeasurable asaṃkhyeya-asaṃkhyeya kalpas, prior to the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eighty-four billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Buddhas; I personally attended upon and made offerings to them all, none of whom were left unattended.
Subhūti! Such immeasurable Buddhas have I all personally served and made offerings to, none of which was in vain.

If, furthermore, there should be someone in a future age, at the end of time, who is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, the merit they obtain would be such that the merit I gained from making offerings to those Buddhas does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal one thousandth, ten thousandth, or ten millionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy.

Subhūti! If there are good men or good women who, in a future age or at the end of the Dharma, receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, were I to fully describe the merit they would obtain, some people upon hearing it would have their minds become deranged, fall into doubt, and fail to believe.
“Subhūti! You should know that this Dharma-gate is inconceivable, and its fruit and retribution are also inconceivable.

Since those who believe in the Hīnayāna and the like cannot hear this, it demonstrates that this is a dharma difficult to hear, yet capable of being believed.

"Those who wish to hear" refers to such phrases as "inconceivable" and so forth.

Regarding the passage on making offerings wherever this sutra may be found: one should know that such a person will certainly accomplish immeasurable merit.

Regarding those who uphold, recite, and read this sutra yet are treated with contempt by others: this demonstrates that they have distanced themselves from all obstacles.

As the verse says, "It is contrary to the path of non-abiding.
As the Sūtra states: "For what reason?"
"Subhūti! In reality, there is no dharma that can be called a bodhisattva who has resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, therefore Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me this prediction, saying: "O māṇava!..."
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
What is called "Tathāgata" is precisely true *tathatā*. Subhūti,
if anyone were to say, "The Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," that person speaks untruthfully.
Subhūti! In truth, there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti!
The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor false within it; therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.
“Subhūti! As for what is called ‘all dharmas,’ all dharmas are indeed not all dharmas; therefore they are called ‘all dharmas.
The Commentary says:
In this regard, a doubt may arise: "If there were no bodhisattvas, how could Śākyamuni Tathāgata have practiced the bodhisattva path under Dīpaṃkara Buddha?
To sever this doubt, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?

and so forth. What meaning does this clarify?
The verse says:
Because he received the prediction at a later time, the practice under Dīpaṃkara was not supreme;
that practice was equal to enlightenment, for it did not possess the characteristics of truly existent conditioned phenomena.

At the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, it was not his first bodhisattva practice. Why is that?
Regarding the various practices I cultivated at that time, there was not a single dharma by which I attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Had I already realized enlightenment under those Buddhas, the subsequent Buddhas would not have bestowed a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon me. If there were no bodhi, there would be no Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
To refute such slander—that is, the claim that Buddhas do not exist at all—the sūtra asks: "For what reason?"
"Subhūti! That which is called 'Tathāgata' is precisely true *tathatā* (suchness).
'True' means it is not erroneous; 'suchness' means it is non-different and immutable."
“Subhūti! If someone were to say:
‘The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,’ what meaning does this indicate?”
The verse says, "Bodhi is equal to those practices.
What is the meaning of this?
If one were to say that those bodhisattva practices possess substantial reality, it would be false.
In this way, when a Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, if someone says that he has "attained" it, this too is false; therefore, it is said that "bodhi is equal to those practices."
If someone were to slander [the teaching] by saying,
"The Tathāgata has not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," in order to sever this doubt, as the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"The Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor false.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because the Tathāgata has attained that bodhi.
The verse states, "It does not possess the characteristics of conditioned phenomena.
The characteristics of conditioned phenomena refer to the characteristics of the five aggregates; however, that dharma of bodhi lacks such characteristics as form and the rest.
Furthermore, how is this so?
The verse says:
That is precisely the mark of non-marks, because it is taught as being non-false.
These dharmas are the dharmas of all Buddhas; they are the essential nature and characteristics of all things.
What is the meaning of this?

It is because those very [dharmas], such as form and so forth, are not characterized by form and so forth, for they possess the characteristic of non-form and so forth; it is because they possess the characteristic of bodhi.
Therefore, the verse says: "That is precisely the markless mark, because it is taught as non-false.
Regarding such statements as, "For this reason, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas," what is the meaning?
Because the Tathāgata has attained such a dharma, as the verse says: "This dharma is the dharma of all Buddhas; it is the self-nature and characteristic of all.
As for "self-nature and characteristic," it is because it is not a substantial self-nature.
What does this clarify? It clarifies that all phenomena have the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) as their essence.
That Dharma is what the Tathāgata has realized; therefore, it is said that "all phenomena are Buddha-dharmas."
Because the characteristics of form and so forth do not abide there, all those phenomena such as form are non-phenomena (*adharma*).
These phenomena being non-phenomena are precisely the reality of phenomena (*dharmatā*), because they lack the characteristics of those phenomena and never maintain or uphold such characteristics.
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body was wondrously vast."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata speaks of the wondrous greatness of the human body, it is not a great body; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name ‘great body.’”
The Commentary says:
What meaning does the analogy of the "Great Body" (mahākāya) manifest?
The verse states:
Based on that Dharmakāya Buddha, the metaphor of the "great body" is taught;
for the body is free from all obscurations and pervades all objects.
Because of its qualities and its great essence, it is therefore called the "great body."
That which is not the body is itself the body; therefore, it is called "not the body.
What do these two verses demonstrate?
They show that [the Buddha] is ultimately free from the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations, and is ultimately endowed with the Dharma-body.
What, then, does this mean?
There are two meanings: first, it pervades all places; [the second is that it is the nature of all phenomena].
Second, its merit is great; therefore, it is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*).
As the verse says: "Merit and the Great Essence.
That which pervades all places means that suchness is undifferentiated across all phenomena (*dharma*).
The verse says: "That which is not the body is itself the body; therefore it is called 'non-body.

When the Tathāgata speaks of the wondrous greatness of the human body, it is not a great body; therefore the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'great body.'"

That which is "not a body" (aśarīra) is so called because it is devoid of all marks;
"great" (mahat) refers to the essence of *tathatā* (suchness). Thus, it is named the "wondrous great body."
As it is said in the Sūtra: "This is called the wondrous great body.

In this regard, there may be doubt: if there were no bodhisattvas, the Buddhas would not attain great enlightenment (mahābodhi), sentient beings would not enter great nirvana (mahāparinirvāṇa), and there would be no pure buddha-fields.
If this is so, for what purpose do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas resolve their minds to lead sentient beings into nirvāṇa, and give rise to the intention to practice in order to purify buddha-fields?
The following scriptural passage serves to resolve this doubt.

The verse says:
Failing to realize the true dharma-realm, yet giving rise to the intention to deliver sentient beings and purify buddha-lands— such a production of mind is itself an inversion.

If giving rise to such a mind constitutes a perversion and disqualifies one from being a bodhisattva, then what kind of mind must be given rise to in order to be called a bodhisattva?
As the sutra says: "Subhūti!..."
"If a bodhisattva thoroughly penetrates non-self and the dharmas that are selfless, the Tathāgata calls him a true bodhisattva, a bodhisattva.

The verse says:
Sentient beings and bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are without self;
this is not the faith of the non-saint’s own wisdom, but rather the wisdom of the saint who possesses it.

Those who know "no-self" and the "dharmas of no-self" refer to sentient beings and bodhisattvas.

One who, regarding those dharmas, possesses self-knowledge and faith—whether through mundane knowledge or supramundane knowledge—be they an ordinary person or a noble one; such a person is called a bodhisattva.

For what reason is that abiding mind called "inverted"?
The verse states: "Because it is devoid of true mindfulness and does not abide in that true wisdom, it is therefore said to be inverted. Thus.
When the Tathāgata says that all dwellings of the mind are non-dwellings of the mind, this phrase demonstrates the distancing from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
What is the meaning of this?
A "dwelling of the mind" refers to dwelling within those foundations of mindfulness; because one has distanced oneself from those foundations of mindfulness, it is called "non-dwelling."
Furthermore, "abiding," "immovability," and "the fundamental" differ in name but are one in meaning.
If it is thus non-abiding, for that reason it is called the "abiding of the mind.

The verse says, "The root of the Buddha’s wisdom.

If it were not the accumulation of merit, the Tathāgata would not have declared it to be the root of wisdom; therefore, the accumulation of merit is indeed the accumulation of merit.

World-Honored One!

The verse states: "Not departing from the dharmadhātu, the teaching of the Dharma has no intrinsic characteristic. Thus it is.

It is because the dharmas that are taught cannot be perceived as having their own specific characteristics apart from the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,

Neither sentient being nor non-sentient being, neither noble nor non-noble.

It is not that they are not sentient beings (*sattva*), for they do possess the body of a noble one.
Such persons are neither ordinary sentient beings, nor are they not sentient beings who possess the body of a noble one.

Thus, compared to this merit, that [other] merit is so slight that there is no analogy whatsoever for it. The Sūtra says: “Subhūti!

The following scriptural passage serves to sever this doubt.
How does one sever doubt?

"Because names are shared with those aggregates, they do not depart from the dharma-realm.

The Buddha said: "Subhūti!

To grasp at "self" and "crossing over" is an error; to grasp at those dharmas is likewise so.

Because the *dharmakāya* of true thusness (*tathatā*) is not an object of consciousness.

One does not lose the causes of merit, nor their superior karmic fruition.
Having attained supreme patience without loss, one obtains the stainless fruit.
To demonstrate the marks of supreme merit, this parable is told;

Some people give rise to such a thought:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because they have attained supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), they lose those merits and their karmic rewards."
To prevent this [misconception], it is shown that merit is not lost, but rather one further attains pure and extraordinary merit; therefore, it is not lost.
As the Sūtra says: "For what reason?"
"Because it is said that 'a bodhisattva who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who knows that all phenomena are without self and attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, they perceive two kinds of selflessness but do not give rise to the marks of these two kinds of selflessness; therefore, they accept [phenomena] without grasping."
As the Sūtra says: “The Buddha said, ‘Subhūti!
A bodhisattva receives merit but does not grasp at merit; for this reason, a bodhisattva takes up merit.’”
Therefore, how does a bodhisattva receive merit without grasping at merit?
The verse says: "This merit has no retribution," because one receives it in such a way as not to grasp it.
What is the meaning of this?
"Grasping" means that those meritorious deeds result in tainted retribution (*sāsrava-vipāka*).
Because they result in tainted retribution, those meritorious deeds are subject to censure.
To grasp in such a manner is called "grasping," because such grasping is not the Path.
Regarding the statement, "This merit has no retribution": "no retribution" means there is no outflowing (āsrava) retribution; therefore, this merit is experienced but not grasped.
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti! If anyone should say, 'The Tathāgata comes or goes, stands, sits, or lies down,' that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught."
"Why is this? A Tathāgata has nowhere to go and nowhere from which he comes; therefore, he is called a Tathāgata.
The Commentary says:
If Bodhisattvas do not experience those karmic fruits, how is it that sentient beings enjoy the merit of the Bodhisattvas?
The verse says:
These fruits of merit should be experienced, yet for the sake of transforming all sentient beings, they do not.
"Spontaneously, through such karma, the Buddhas appear throughout the ten directions.
What is the meaning of this?
It clarifies that the emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddhas have utility, for those Buddhas of the Dharma body (*dharmakāya*) neither go nor come.
The verse says: "By the natural power of such karma, the Buddhas manifest throughout the ten directions.
What, then, is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
The transformation-body Buddhas of the past and future, and the Tathāgata who is eternally unmoving—
within this realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they are neither one nor different.
This clarifies the meaning of neither going nor coming.
As the Sūtra says: "For what reason?
Because the Tathāgata has nowhere to go and nowhere from which he comes.
What is the meaning of this?
If the Tathāgata were subject to the distinction of coming and going, one could not say that he dwells eternally thus.
To dwell eternally thus means to be neither changing nor different.
The Sūtra says:

“Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the atoms of a trichiliocosm, and then further grind as many worlds as there are those atoms into incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers of atoms.”
Subhūti, what do you think? Would that multitude of atoms be considered many?
Subhūti said: "That multitude of atoms is very great,
World-Honored One!"
Why is this? If these multitudes of atoms were substantially existent, the Buddha would not have spoken of them as "multitudes of atoms. Why is this?
The Buddha spoke of a multitude of atoms, yet they are not a multitude of atoms; therefore, the Buddha spoke of a multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One!
That which the Tathāgata has spoken of as a trichiliocosm is not a world; therefore, the Buddha spoke of a trichiliocosm.
Why is this? If a world were truly existent, it would be a "single integrated mark.
What the Tathāgata calls a single integrated mark is not actually a single integrated mark; therefore, the Buddha speaks of a single integrated mark.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! That which is a unified whole is ineffable; it is only ordinary people who greedily cling to such things.”
Why is this? Subhūti! If someone should speak thus:
“The Buddha has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being,
and the view of a life-span. Subhūti, what do you think?
"Is what this person says correct speech? Subhūti replied, "No."
World-Honored One!
Why is this? World-Honored One!

When the Tathāgata speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, these are not actually views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; they are merely designated as "the view of a self," "the view of a person," "the view of a sentient being," and "the view of a life-span."

“Subhūti! A bodhisattva who has resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should know all dharmas in this way, see them in this way, and believe in them in this way; thus they do not dwell upon the characteristics of dharmas.”

Why is this? Subhūti, that which is called the "characteristic of dharmas" has been taught by the Tathāgata as being no characteristic of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "characteristic of dharmas."
Subhūti! If there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who took seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offered them as a gift;

and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has set their mind on awakening (bodhicitta) and, from this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, were to receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain even so much as a four-line verse for others—their merit would surpass that of the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas.
"How so? To expound for others while not speaking, this is called 'speaking.
The Commentary says:
What meaning does the simile of crushing [the world] into atoms demonstrate?
The verse says:
"The world is made into atoms; this simile demonstrates that meaning."
Reducing even a mote of dust to powder demonstrates the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*).
What does this clarify?
The verse says: "Within this realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is neither unity nor difference."

Those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not abide in a single location within the *dharmadhātu* of true thusness (*tathatā*), nor do they abide in separate locations; it is to demonstrate this meaning that the analogy of the world being reduced to minute atoms is taught.
What meaning does this metaphor illustrate?
A verse states: "Reducing atoms to dust illustrates the exhaustion of afflictions.
This metaphor does not refer to a collection of atoms; rather, it illustrates that [the subject] is not a single entity.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
It is a collection because it is not a collection; it is not merely a single metaphor.
The place of aggregation is not that [atom], nor is it a distinct metaphor.
What is the meaning of this?
It is like when a minute particle is ground into powder; it does not abide in a single location because there is no longer any aggregated substance.
Nor is there a distinction of different locations, because a distinction among the accumulated atoms cannot be apprehended, and because such distinctions do not abide.
Thus, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, having distanced themselves from the hindrance of afflictions, dwell within that dharmadhātu; they do not dwell in one place, nor do they dwell in different places.
This analogy of the "single unified mass" (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa) of the trichiliocosm is not [to be understood as] a mere collection. For what reason?
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata speaks of the single unified mass, yet it is not a single unified mass; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of the single unified mass."
If there were truly a single entity that was a collection, the Tathāgata would not speak of a collection of atoms.
Likewise, if there were truly a single world-system, the Tathāgata would not speak of a trichiliocosm.

As the Sūtra states: "If a world were truly existent, it would be a single unified mass; however, only foolish commoners are greedily attached to such things. This is because that which is an aggregation has no substance that can be grasped; it is a false conceptualization, and for this reason, foolish commoners grasp at it falsely.
If there were anything real, that would be right view; therefore, we know it is a false grasping.
Why? Because ordinary people grasp at things where there are no things.
As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha said, 'Subhūti!
That which is a unified whole (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa) is inexpressible; it is only ordinary people who greedily cling to such things. What meaning does this demonstrate?
The verse says:
Ordinary beings grasp at perversions merely by following sounds;
they do not attain the Way through non-duality, for they remain far removed from my Dharma.
As the sutra says: "For what reason?
Subhūti, if someone were to speak thus:"

For the Buddha has said: "The view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span—these, and so forth, are called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span."
What is the meaning of this?
The verse states: "The Way is not attained through non-duality; it is far removed from self and dharmas.
What is the significance of this?
It is not that there is no self or no dharmas; rather, one attains bodhi by being free from these two things.
How is bodhi attained? One attains bodhi by remaining far removed from those two views.
The verse says, "Distant from my Dharma.
What, then, is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
To see me is to not see me; it is a false vision devoid of reality.
This is a subtle obstruction, which is abandoned upon seeing suchness.

Therefore, to see is to not see, for there is no real meaning [in it]. Because it is a false conceptualization and because it is without self, the Tathāgata says that this view of self is actually non-seeing, as it lacks reality.
That which lacks reality is precisely non-existence.
For this reason, it is said that the view of self is itself a false view.
By thus demonstrating that the view of self is non-seeing, one who views dharmas is likewise non-seeing.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Subhūti!

A bodhisattva who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should know all phenomena in this way, see them in this way, and believe in them in this way; thus they do not dwell upon the marks of phenomena."
What is the meaning of this?
It is because seeing the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is itself not seeing characteristics, just as that view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is itself not a [valid] vision.
For what reason are these two views called "not seeing"?
The verse states: "This is a subtle obstruction; by seeing suchness, one is far removed from it.
What does this mean?
That one perceives a self and perceives dharmas—this is the subtle obstruction.
Because those two are not seen, one attains detachment through the vision of the Dharma;
as the verse says, "Seeing suchness, one is detached.
Furthermore, what is the meaning indicated by "knowing thus, seeing thus, and believing thus"?
The verse says:
Through the two wisdoms and samādhi, one thus attains detachment;
the emanation body manifests merit, yet it is not devoid of inexhaustible merit.
What is the meaning of this?
It demonstrates mundane wisdom and ultimate wisdom, as well as how one attains detachment from those obstacles by relying on samādhi; for this reason, the analogy of supreme merit is stated again.
What meaning does this demonstrate?
The verse states: "The emanation body manifests merit; it is not that inexhaustible merit is absent.
What, then, is the meaning of this?

Although all Buddhas naturally manifest transformation bodies to perform their activities, those transformation bodies of the Buddhas preach the Dharma because they possess immeasurable, inexhaustible, and untainted merit.
How is it that one expounds for others without this being called "expounding," yet it is nevertheless called "expounding"?
For what reason is it said thus?
The verse says:
When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do not say, "This is an emanation body.
Because they do not speak in such a manner, their teaching is correct.
What is the meaning of this?
When the emanation-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do not say, "I am an emanation-body. Therefore, what they teach is the authentic teaching.
If they were not to speak in this manner, the sentient beings to be transformed would fail to give rise to a mind of reverence.
Why is this? Because it cannot benefit sentient beings, that which is said is called an incorrect teaching; therefore, I do not say that I am a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*).
The Sūtra says:
"All conditioned phenomena are like stars, a cataract, a lamp, a magical illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud; one should contemplate them in this way."
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, there may be doubt: if all Buddha-Tathāgatas constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, why is it said that the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa?
To sever this doubt, the Tathāgata spoke those verses and parables.
What is their meaning?
The verse says:
The nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas is neither conditioned nor separate [from it];
for by means of sublime wisdom they correctly contemplate the nine kinds of conditioned phenomena.
What is the meaning of this?
The nirvāṇa of all Buddhas is neither a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) nor is it separate from conditioned phenomena. Why is this?
Because when the Buddhas attain nirvāṇa, they manifest emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) that preach the Dharma and display worldly conduct for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
This clarifies that because the Buddhas do not abide in nirvana and do not abide in the world.
Why? Because although the Buddhas manifest worldly conduct, they do not abide within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The verse states: "Because the ninefold conditioned phenomena are correctly contemplated by sublime wisdom. What is the meaning of this?
It refers to the correct contemplation of the ninefold [phenomena] as being like stars and other relative phenomena.
These nine kinds of correct contemplation should be understood in relation to nine kinds of objects.
What are the objects of contemplation?
The verse says:
The perceived object, the perceiving consciousness, The vessel-world, the body, and the objects of enjoyment,
As well as past and present phenomena— One likewise contemplates the future world.
How does one contemplate these nine kinds of phenomena?
For example, just as the stars are present yet do not appear when eclipsed by the sun,
so too is it with the mind and its phenomena that can be perceived.
Furthermore, just as one with a cataract in the eye sees such things as floating hairs, so too does one perceive conditioned phenomena, due to inverted views.
Furthermore, consciousness is like a lamp, because it abides by depending on the phenomena of craving and attachment.
Moreover, it is like the locus upon which an illusion depends, because the various distinctions of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) lack a single, real essence.
Furthermore, it is like dew on the body, for it abides only for a short time.
It is also like a bubble; the objects of experience are likewise so, because the three factors—the sensation, perception, and cause—are unstable.
Furthermore, just as a dream, so too are past phenomena, because they exist only as mental recollections.
Furthermore, just as lightning, so too are present phenomena, because they do not abide for even a single moment.
Furthermore, just as with clouds, so it is with future dharmas; for at the time of the seed, the ālayavijñāna serves as the fundamental seed for all dharmas.
By contemplating these nine kinds of phenomena, what merits are attained and what wisdom is accomplished?
The verse says:
Contemplating characteristics and enjoyments, And contemplating the events of the three periods of time.
Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one attains stainless mastery (*vibhutva*).
What is the meaning of this?
One contemplates three aspects of conditioned phenomena:
First, one contemplates conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) by contemplating their characteristics and consciousness.

Second, one contemplates experience (*upabhoga*), by contemplating the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) and so forth: in what place does one dwell, with what kind of body, and what is it that is experienced?
Third is the contemplation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*): by what dharmas do they undergo differentiation through the transformation of the three periods of time?
One contemplates all dharmas in this manner because one attains mastery over worldly phenomena.
The verse says: "Within conditioned phenomena, one attains stainless mastery.
Thus the Sūtra states:
"After the Buddha had spoken this sūtra..."

The Venerable Subhūti, along with all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The rare dhāraṇī-dharma of all Buddhas, Its profound phrases and meanings are beyond measure;
Having heard this from the Venerable One and its extensive exposition, I dedicate this merit to all living beings.
Treatise on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll II.
